passage.text: The people below want to choose from travel planning, local transport and holiday services. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Guided day trip to the coastal village of Wrenmouth — Join us every Saturday for a full-day excursion along the clifftop path to Wrenmouth harbour. The coach leaves the town centre at eight sharp and returns by six. A local guide shares stories about smuggling history, and there is free time for lunch at the fish market. Walking shoes are essential as the path is uneven.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Monthly travel photography walk for beginners — Bring any camera or phone and learn to capture stations, bridges and cityscapes. A professional photographer leads a gentle two-hour walk on the first Sunday of each month, stopping at five viewpoints. Participants receive a printed tip sheet afterwards. No booking needed; just meet outside the main entrance at nine.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Evening language café for travellers — Worried about ordering food abroad or asking for directions? Drop into this relaxed Thursday session where volunteers help you practise holiday phrases in French, Spanish or Italian. Each meeting focuses on one situation, such as checking into a hotel or buying train tickets. Tea is provided and attendance is free.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Weekend cycle route planning workshop — By the end of this three-hour Saturday workshop, you will have mapped a safe cycling route for your next holiday. An instructor shows how to read contour maps, find traffic-free paths and pack a repair kit. Participants leave with a personalised route card. Bring a laptop or tablet; maps are provided.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Accessible minibus service for disabled passengers — Designed for wheelchair users and passengers with limited mobility, this door-to-door service operates weekdays between eight and five. Drivers are trained in assistance, and vehicles have ramps and securement points. Book at least one day ahead by phone or online. Fares match the standard bus price.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Budget airline comparison masterclass — If you have ever paid too much for a short flight, this ninety-minute online session reveals how fares change and when to book. A travel journalist explains hidden fees, luggage rules and the best days to fly. Attendees receive a comparison checklist. The class runs on three Wednesday evenings in March.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Heritage railway volunteer experience — Every second Saturday from April to October, volunteers help run a steam train between Millbrook and Fernham. Roles include ticket checking, platform announcing and tea serving. No experience is needed; a training morning is provided in March. Volunteers travel free on any service day and receive a discounted season pass.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Family camping and navigation weekend — At Greenfield Activity Centre, families spend two nights under canvas learning to navigate by map and compass. Days include a guided hill walk, an evening campfire and a morning orienteering challenge. All equipment is supplied, and instructors hold outdoor leadership certificates. Suitable for children aged eight and above.

questions.prompt: Sofia uses a wheelchair and needs to reach a hospital appointment across town on a Tuesday. She wants a service that picks her up at home and charges the same as the regular bus.
Tom always overpays for flights and wants to understand fares better. He can attend online on weekday evenings and would like a written checklist to keep.
Priya is nervous about her first trip to Spain and cannot speak any Spanish. She wants a free, relaxed group where she can practise ordering meals and asking for directions.
Marcus loves steam trains and has free time on alternate Saturdays. He would enjoy a practical role outdoors and does not mind attending a training session beforehand.
The Chen family wants an outdoor weekend for their two children, aged nine and twelve. They have no camping gear and need qualified staff to teach map reading.

passage.text: When the commuters in our town started a cycle routes project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving safe paths. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

parts.passageTitle: Part 4 – Volunteering at an animal shelter

passage.text: I started volunteering at an animal shelter during the school holidays last summer. (16) ..... The shelter cared for over fifty cats and dogs, and the staff were always busy looking after the animals. The shelter relied entirely on donations from the public and the hard work of volunteers, so every hour I spent there made a real difference to the animals and the staff.

My main job was cleaning the cages and refilling food and water bowls every morning. (17) ..... It was not a glamorous task, but I could see how much the animals appreciated the attention and care they received from the volunteers. I learned to be patient and gentle with frightened animals, understanding that they needed time to trust humans again after whatever difficult experiences they had been through.

One day, a young dog arrived who had been injured in a road accident and was very frightened. (18) ..... The vet came twice a week to check on his progress, and I was allowed to help during the treatments by holding the dog still. I sat with him for hours each day, speaking softly and offering treats until he began to trust me enough to let me touch him and check his injuries properly.

Watching the dog recover and eventually find a new home was incredibly rewarding for me. (19) ..... Seeing him leave with a caring family made all the hard work worthwhile and showed me the difference we can make. The experience of helping an injured animal recover and find a loving home gave me a sense of purpose and showed me that my efforts could have a direct impact on another creature.

Volunteering at the shelter completely changed my perspective on animal welfare and care. (20) ..... I now hope to become a veterinarian so I can help animals professionally and make a real difference in their lives. I also learned that animals need patience rather than attention all the time, because a quiet approach often helps a frightened animal feel safe enough to respond.

We had been training (21) ..... early morning sessions for weeks before the big match arrived. The team we faced had (22) ..... lost a game all season, so we knew it would be a tough challenge. Our coach told us to focus (23) ..... playing as a team rather than trying to be individual stars on the court. In the final quarter, we were five points behind, (24) ..... we did not give up and kept fighting until the end. With thirty seconds left, our captain scored the winning basket. The crowd cheered (25) ..... loudly that you could hear them across the whole sports centre. It was (26) ..... unforgettable experience for everyone on the team and for our supporters. The victory was celebrated by the whole school, and our team was invited to represent the region in the national championship next month, which is an incredible honour for all of us. The coach explained that good care also means observing an animal quietly. I learned to notice small changes in behaviour, and this made my daily work at the shelter more careful.
